newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Reserve Bank lifting forward cover prices.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Reserve Bank lifting forward cover prices.

text.p: South Africa's Reserve Bank was increasing prices for providing forward foreign exchange cover in a bid to cut its exposure, Governor Chris Stals told parliament's finance committee on Friday.

"We can make the price of forward cover more and more expensive and so discourage the private sector from coming to the Reserve Bank to make use of the forward cover, and this we certainly do," he said.

"Every time we feel there is an opportunity to reduce the forward book, we make the price from the Reserve Bank more expensive which makes it more economical and profitable for the (commercial) banks to take over the business."

Stals noted the oversold forward position of the central bank -- which offers cover on behalf of the government -- had increased to some $20 billion this year from $8 billion a year or so ago. But this was now declining and would continue to do so if South Africans believed the rand was stabilising.
At the same time the banks were taking on more of the business and now accounted for around half the forward cover market.
Finance department director general Maria Ramos earlier told the same committee that the government's commitment to better debt management included reduced exposure to the forward cover market.
It had been decided to stop providing long term forward cover at subsidised rates to parastatals and the Reserve Bank aimed eventually to withdraw from the forward cover market entirely.
"Developments around exchange control in the budget would create an environment in which the Reserve Bank would reduce, on a managed basis, its participation," Ramos said.
At the same time the government was restructuring its debt management to transfer risk in the bond market to the banks.
The first phase would be to ring fence Reserve Bank activities related to government funding so there was a better picture on a daily basis of what its funding position was.
The second phase would be to move away from the situation in which the Reserve Bank and the department of finance bought and sold government stock.
The aim would be to appoint primary dealers which meant that banks would take the risk.

Ramos noted this would require several structural changes, including the shortening of settlement periods. These were currently 14 days while the international norm was three days and in some cases settlements were done immediately.
"We are going to be pursuing that very actively...It is exceedingly important that we address this issue, particularly as our markets open up," she said.
Consideration was also being given to a move from a tap to an auction system.
